goals: Classify forces as contact or non-contact and state the inverse square dependence of non-contact forces on distance
Convert between newton, dyne, kgf and gf
State Newton’s first law and explain inertia of rest and of motion

slides.heading: What is a force?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — a force is a push or a pull. It can start or stop a motion, change its speed or direction, or change the shape of a body.

visual.alt: Flow: force, changes motion or shape, laws of motion

slides.narration: A push or a pull is a force. A force can set a body moving, bring it to rest, speed it up, slow it down, turn it, or change its shape. Newton gave three laws that tell us how force and motion are linked.

slides.heading: Contact forces
slides.body_md: A **contact force** acts only when two bodies touch. Examples: **friction** (opposes sliding), **normal reaction** (the support pushing back, at right angles to the surface) and **tension** (the pull of a stretched string).

slides.heading: Units of force: newton and dyne
slides.body_md: The **newton (N)** is the SI unit: the force that gives a mass of **1 kg** an acceleration of **1 m s⁻²**. The **dyne** is the cgs unit: the force that gives **1 g** an acceleration of **1 cm s⁻²**. **1 N = 10⁵ dyne**.

visual.alt: Table of the newton and the dyne with their definitions

slides.narration: One newton is the force that gives one kilogram an acceleration of one metre per second squared. One dyne does the same for one gram and one centimetre per second squared. One newton equals one hundred thousand dynes.

slides.heading: Gravitational units: kgf and gf
slides.body_md: The **kilogram-force (kgf)** is the force with which the Earth pulls a mass of 1 kg: **1 kgf = 9.8 N** (10 N if the question says g = 10). **1 gf** is the pull on 1 g: **1 gf = 980 dyne**. Also 1 kgf = 1000 gf.

visual.alt: Table of conversions between newton, dyne, kgf and gf

slides.narration: A kilogram force is the weight of one kilogram, so it equals nine point eight newtons. A gram force is the weight of one gram, which is nine hundred and eighty dynes. These units are used only for conversion here.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: converting units of force
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Convert (a) 4 kgf to N, (b) 2.5 N to dyne, (c) 250 gf to N. (1 kgf = 9.8 N; 1 N = $10^5$ dyne; 1 gf = 980 dyne)

**Step 1.** $4 \times 9.8 = 39.2$ N.

**Step 2.** $2.5 \times 10^5 = 250000$ dyne.

**Step 3.** $250 \times 980 = 245000$ dyne $= \dfrac{245000}{100000} = 2.45$ N.

visual.alt: Table showing three conversions of force units

slides.narration: Choose the conversion factor and multiply. Four kilogram force is thirty nine point two newtons. Two point five newtons is two hundred and fifty thousand dynes. Two hundred and fifty gram force is two hundred and forty five thousand dynes, or two point four five newtons.

slides.heading: Newton’s first law and inertia
slides.body_md: **Newton’s first law:** a body continues in its state of **rest** or of **uniform motion in a straight line** unless an **external force** acts on it. This tendency to stay as it is is **inertia**; a force is what **changes** this state. **Inertia of rest:** the coin stays when the card is flicked away.

slides.heading: Inertia of motion in everyday life
slides.body_md: **Inertia of motion:** a moving body tends to keep moving. When a bus **brakes suddenly**, the passenger’s body **lurches forward**. Other examples: dust leaves a beaten carpet; a rider is thrown forward when a cycle stops suddenly. **Dynamic inertia** is inertia of motion; **static inertia** is inertia of rest.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the inverse square law
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Two charged balls attract each other with a force of 36 N when they are 1 m apart. Find the force when the distance is made 3 m. (The force varies as $\dfrac{1}{r^2}$.)

**Step 1.** Distance becomes 3 times, so the force becomes $\dfrac{1}{3^2} = \dfrac{1}{9}$ of its value.

**Step 2.** New force $= \dfrac{36}{9} = 4$ N.

slides.narration: If the distance becomes three times, the force becomes one over three squared, which is one ninth. One ninth of thirty six newtons is four newtons.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Contact forces: friction, normal reaction, tension. Non-contact forces: gravitational, electric, magnetic (inverse square for many).
Units: 1 N = 10⁵ dyne; 1 kgf = 9.8 N; 1 gf = 980 dyne; 1 kgf = 1000 gf.
First law: a body keeps its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless an external force acts; this property is inertia.
Inertia of rest (static) and inertia of motion (dynamic) explain many everyday events.

visual.alt: Summary table of contact and non-contact forces

slides.narration: To sum up. Forces may need contact or not. The newton and the dyne are the absolute units, and the kilogram force and gram force are gravitational units. The first law says a body keeps its state unless a force acts, and that tendency is inertia.

goals: Define linear momentum and show that force equals the rate of change of momentum, which is ma for constant mass
Solve simple numerical problems combining F = ma with the equations of motion
Identify action-reaction pairs and explain why they do not cancel

slides.heading: From momentum to force
slides.body_md: Part 2 — heavier and faster bodies are harder to stop. Momentum measures this, and force is how fast momentum changes.

visual.alt: Flow: momentum, second law, third law pairs

slides.narration: A heavy lorry is harder to stop than a bicycle at the same speed. Momentum measures this. Newton’s second law links force to the rate of change of momentum, and the third law tells us forces come in pairs.

slides.heading: Linear momentum
slides.body_md: **Linear momentum** is the product of **mass and velocity**: **p = mv**. It is a **vector** in the direction of the velocity. SI unit: **kg m s⁻¹**; cgs unit: g cm s⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of the momentum of a ball and of a trolley

slides.narration: Momentum is mass times velocity. A cricket ball of zero point one five kilogram at twenty metres per second has a momentum of three kilogram metres per second. Momentum has the direction of the velocity.

slides.heading: The second law: F = ma
slides.body_md:
**Second law:** the **rate of change of momentum** is proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of the force.

For a body of constant mass $m$ whose velocity changes from $u$ to $v$ in time $t$:

$F = \dfrac{mv - mu}{t} = m \dfrac{v - u}{t} = ma$.

visual.alt: Table of the definition of the newton and the dyne from the second law

slides.narration: Force is the rate of change of momentum. For a body of constant mass, the change in momentum is mass times the change in velocity, so force equals mass times acceleration. This also defines the newton and the dyne.

slides.heading: Quick check: F = ma
slides.body_md: Divide the force by the mass.

visual.alt: Table giving a force and a mass

slides.narration: A force of twenty newtons acts on a body of mass eight kilograms. What is the acceleration?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: F = ma with equations of motion
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A car of mass 800 kg is pushed from rest by a force of 1200 N. Find its speed and the distance covered in 5 s.

**Step 1.** $a = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{1200}{800} = 1.5$ m s⁻².

**Step 2.** $v = u + at = 0 + 1.5 \times 5 = 7.5$ m s⁻¹.

**Step 3.** $S = \dfrac{1}{2}at^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1.5 \times 25 = 18.75$ m.

visual.alt: Table of the data and answers for the car

slides.narration: First use the second law to get the acceleration, one point five metres per second squared. Then use the equations of motion from the last chapter for the speed and the distance.

slides.heading: Quick check: force and motion
slides.body_md: Find the acceleration first, then use an equation of motion.

visual.alt: Table giving force, mass, starting condition and time

slides.narration: A force of one hundred and fifty newtons acts on a body of mass fifty kilograms starting from rest for four seconds. What is its final velocity?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: force from a change of momentum
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A car of mass 1000 kg moving at 15 m s⁻¹ is brought to rest in 5 s. Find the retarding force and the distance covered.

**Step 1.** $a = \dfrac{0 - 15}{5} = -3$ m s⁻².

**Step 2.** $F = ma = 1000 \times (-3) = -3000$ N, so the retarding force is 3000 N opposite to the motion.

**Step 3.** $S = \dfrac{u + v}{2} \times t = 7.5 \times 5 = 37.5$ m.

visual.alt: Table of the change of momentum, time, force and distance of the braking car

slides.narration: The momentum falls by fifteen thousand kilogram metres per second in five seconds, so the force is three thousand newtons against the motion. The distance is the average velocity times the time, thirty seven point five metres.

slides.heading: Why a fielder draws the hands back
slides.body_md: Stopping a ball of mass 0.16 kg moving at 25 m s⁻¹ means removing a momentum of **4 kg m s⁻¹**. **F = change of momentum ÷ time**: in **0.05 s** the force is **80 N**; in **0.2 s** it is only **20 N**. A longer time means a smaller force, so the hands hurt less.

slides.narration: When one body pushes another, the second body pushes back with an equal force in the opposite direction. The two forces act on different bodies. The push on the wall and the push on the boy are one such pair.

slides.heading: Pairs in walking, rowing and rockets
slides.body_md: **Walking:** the foot pushes the ground backward; the ground pushes the foot forward. **Rowing:** the oar pushes the water backward; the water pushes the boat forward. **Rocket:** the rocket pushes the gases down; the gases push the rocket up.

slides.narration: In walking, the foot pushes the ground back and the ground pushes you forward. A boat moves forward because the oar pushes water back. A rocket burns fuel and throws gas downward, and the gas pushes the rocket upward.

slides.heading: Why action and reaction do not cancel
slides.body_md: Two forces cancel only if they act on the **same body**. Action and reaction act on **different bodies**, so each one produces its own effect. Your push on a trolley acts on the trolley; the trolley’s push acts on you.

rows: Weight and normal reaction on a book
Push of boy on wall and push of wall on boy

visual.alt: Table comparing forces on one body with an action-reaction pair

slides.narration: Forces cancel only when they act on one body. The action and its reaction act on two different bodies, so they cannot cancel each other, and each causes its own motion.

slides.body_md: A pair acts on two different bodies.

visual.alt: Table giving an action and asking for its reaction

slides.narration: A hammer hits a nail. Which force is the reaction to the force of the hammer on the nail?

slides.heading: Worked example 3: finding a pair in a situation
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A boy of mass 40 kg stands on the ground and pushes a wall with a force of 120 N. (a) Name the reaction. (b) Give its magnitude and direction. (c) Why does the wall not move away even though 120 N acts on it?

**Step 1.** Action: force of the boy on the wall. Reaction: **force of the wall on the boy**.

**Step 2.** Magnitude $= 120$ N, opposite in direction to the push on the wall.

**Step 3.** The wall is fixed to the ground; friction at its base balances the push, so the net force on it is zero.

visual.alt: Table of the action and reaction forces between the boy and the wall

slides.narration: The reaction to the boy pushing the wall is the wall pushing the boy. It is equal to one hundred and twenty newtons and acts in the opposite direction. The wall stays still because other forces on it balance the push.

bullets: Momentum p = mv (vector); unit kg m s⁻¹.
Second law: F = rate of change of momentum = ma for constant mass; 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻²; 1 dyne = 1 g cm s⁻².
A longer stopping time means a smaller force for the same change of momentum.
Third law: action and reaction are equal, opposite, act on different bodies and so do not cancel.

rows: no force, no change in the state of motion
equal and opposite forces on different bodies

visual.alt: Summary table of Newton’s three laws

slides.narration: To sum up. Momentum is mass times velocity. Force equals mass times acceleration, which is the rate of change of momentum. A longer time to stop means a smaller force. And action and reaction are equal and opposite and act on different bodies.

sections.heading: 2. Units of force
sections.body_md:
The **newton (N)** is the SI unit of force: the force that gives a body of mass **1 kg** an acceleration of **1 m s⁻²**, so 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻². The **dyne** is the cgs unit: the force that gives **1 g** an acceleration of **1 cm s⁻²**, so 1 dyne = 1 g cm s⁻².

**1 N = 10⁵ dyne.**

**Gravitational units.** The **kilogram-force (kgf)** is the force (weight) with which the Earth attracts a mass of 1 kg: **1 kgf = 9.8 N** (take 10 N if the question says g = 10 m s⁻²). The **gram-force (gf)** is the pull on 1 g: **1 gf = 980 dyne**; 1 kgf = 1000 gf.

| Conversion | Value |
|---|---|
| 4 kgf to N | 4 × 9.8 = 39.2 N |
| 2.5 N to dyne | 2.5 × 10⁵ = 250000 dyne |
| 250 gf to dyne | 250 × 980 = 245000 dyne |

kgf and gf are used in this course only for conversions; second-law numericals use newton or dyne.

key_terms.definition_md: The force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻².
The force that gives a mass of 1 g an acceleration of 1 cm s⁻².
The force with which the Earth attracts a mass of 1 kg; 1 kgf = 9.8 N.

sections.heading: 3. Newton’s first law and inertia
sections.body_md:
**First law:** a body continues in its state of **rest** or of **uniform motion in a straight line** unless it is acted on by an **external (unbalanced) force**.

**Inertia** is the property of a body by which it **resists any change** in its state of rest or of uniform motion. The first law therefore also **defines force**: a force is that which changes, or tends to change, the state of rest or of uniform motion of a body.

- **Inertia of rest (static inertia):** a body at rest tends to stay at rest. A coin on a card stays in place when the card is flicked sharply and drops into the tumbler; passengers fall backward when a bus starts suddenly.
- **Inertia of motion (dynamic inertia):** a moving body tends to keep moving. A passenger lurches forward when a bus brakes; dust flies out of a beaten carpet; a runner cannot stop at once.

When the net force on a body is zero it moves with constant velocity (or stays at rest); no force is needed to keep it moving steadily once the friction is removed.

key_terms.definition_md: The property of a body by which it resists a change in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line.
That which changes or tends to change the state of rest or of uniform motion of a body.

sections.heading: 4. Momentum and the second law
sections.body_md:
**Linear momentum** *p* = mass × velocity = **mv**; it is a vector in the direction of the velocity. SI unit **kg m s⁻¹**; cgs unit g cm s⁻¹. A cricket ball of 0.15 kg at 20 m s⁻¹ has p = 3 kg m s⁻¹.

**Second law:** the **rate of change of momentum** of a body is proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of the force. For a body of **constant mass** whose velocity changes from u to v in time t:

F ∝ (mv − mu) ÷ t = m(v − u) ÷ t = ma, and with the units chosen so that the constant is 1: **F = ma**. This defines the newton and the dyne.

**Combining with the equations of motion.** Find a = F ÷ m first, then use v = u + at or S = ut + ½at². A car of 800 kg pushed from rest by 1200 N has a = 1.5 m s⁻², v = 7.5 m s⁻¹ and S = 18.75 m after 5 s. A 1000 kg car stopped from 15 m s⁻¹ in 5 s needs a force of 3000 N.

**Application: catching a ball.** The change of momentum is fixed; the force is (change of momentum) ÷ time. A fielder draws the hands back to **increase the time**, so the **force on the hands is smaller**: for a ball of 0.16 kg moving at 25 m s⁻¹ the force is 80 N in 0.05 s but only 20 N in 0.2 s. The same idea explains cushions, sand beds for jumpers and the bending of knees on landing.

In cgs units F is in dyne, m in g and a in cm s⁻²: 5 × 10⁴ dyne on 250 g gives a = 200 cm s⁻².

key_terms.definition_md: The product of the mass and the velocity of a body; a vector quantity.
The rate of change of momentum of a body is proportional to the force applied and is in the direction of the force.

sections.heading: 5. Newton’s third law
sections.body_md:
**Third law:** to every **action** there is an **equal and opposite reaction**.

The action and the reaction:
- are **equal in size** and **opposite in direction**;
- act on **two different bodies**;
- act at the **same time**, and are forces of the **same kind**.

**Pairs in everyday life.** *Walking:* the foot pushes the ground backward (action), the ground pushes the foot forward (reaction). *Rowing:* the oar pushes the water backward, the water pushes the boat forward. *Rocket:* it pushes the exhaust gases downward at high speed, the gases push the rocket upward. A boy pushing a wall with 120 N receives a push of 120 N from the wall.

**Why they do not cancel.** Two forces cancel each other only when they act on the **same body**. The action and the reaction act on **different bodies**, so each causes its own effect. (The weight of a book and the normal reaction of the table are *not* an action-reaction pair: they act on the same body.)

key_terms.definition_md: The pair of equal and opposite forces that two interacting bodies exert on each other; they act on different bodies.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Treating kgf as the SI unit, or writing 1 kgf = 9.8 dyne instead of 9.8 N.
- Using grams or centimetres in F = ma with a force in newtons without converting.
- Saying that a force is needed to keep a body moving at a steady speed (the first law says no net force is needed).
- Saying that action and reaction cancel; they act on different bodies.
- Taking the weight of a book and the normal reaction of the table as an action-reaction pair (they act on the same body).
- Forgetting that momentum is a vector, and giving no unit with an answer.
- In the fielder question, saying the force is smaller because the momentum is smaller; the change of momentum is the same, the time is longer.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a definition, a unit or a conversion.
- 2 marks: a numerical with the formula, substitution and unit.
- 3 marks: a reasoned answer in three points, or a two-step calculation.
- 10-mark structured question: parts on a situation or figure: write F = ma or the momentum formula, substitute, use an equation of motion where needed, and give units; name the action and reaction pair with the body each force acts on.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A body continues in its state of **rest** or of **uniform motion in a straight line** unless an **external force** acts on it.

**(b)** The coin is at rest and tends to **remain at rest** when the card is removed quickly; with no support below it, gravity pulls it down into the tumbler. This is **inertia of rest** (static inertia).

**(c)** The feet are stopped with the bus by friction, but the upper body tends to **keep moving forward** with the earlier velocity, so the passenger lurches forward. This is **inertia of motion** (dynamic inertia).

**(d)** When the car stops suddenly, the occupants tend to **keep moving forward** because of inertia of motion; the belt exerts a **force that stops them** and prevents injury.

questions.solution_md: First law; inertia of rest; inertia of motion; seat belts oppose forward motion.

A truck of mass 2000 kg changes its speed from 5 m s⁻¹ to 12 m s⁻¹ in 7 s.

(a) Define linear momentum and state its SI unit. [2]

(b) State Newton’s second law and use it to show that F = ma for a body of constant mass. [3]

(c) Find the change in momentum of the truck and the force that acts on it. [3]

(d) Find the acceleration of the truck and verify that F = ma gives the same force. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Linear momentum is the **product of mass and velocity**, p = mv; its SI unit is **kg m s⁻¹**.

**(b)** The **rate of change of momentum** of a body is proportional to the applied force and is in the direction of the force. F ∝ (mv − mu) ÷ t = m(v − u) ÷ t = ma, so **F = ma**.

**(c)** Change of momentum = 2000 × (12 − 5) = **14000 kg m s⁻¹**; F = 14000 ÷ 7 = **2000 N**.

**(d)** a = (12 − 5) ÷ 7 = **1 m s⁻²**; F = ma = 2000 × 1 = **2000 N**, the same.

questions.solution_md: p = mv, kg m/s; second law and F = ma; 14000 kg m/s and 2000 N; 1 m/s², 2000 N.

questions.stem_md:

(a) Find the momentum of the ball before it is caught. [2]

(b) Find the average force on the hands if the ball is stopped in 0.04 s with the hands held fixed. [2]

(c) Find the average force if the hands are drawn back and the ball takes 0.14 s to stop. [2]

(d) Find how many times larger the first force is than the second, and explain why the fielder draws the hands back. [2]

(e) Give one other example in which a longer stopping time is used to reduce a force. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** p = mv = 0.14 × 30 = **4.2 kg m s⁻¹**.

**(b)** F = change of momentum ÷ time = 4.2 ÷ 0.04 = **105 N**.

**(c)** F = 4.2 ÷ 0.14 = **30 N**.

**(d)** 105 ÷ 30 = **3.5 times**. The change of momentum is the same, so a **longer time** gives a **smaller force** and the hands are not hurt.

**(e)** A high jumper lands on a thick foam mat (or: bending the knees on landing; cushions in vehicles); the longer stopping time reduces the force.

questions.solution_md: 4.2 kg m/s; 105 N; 30 N; 3.5 times, longer time smaller force; foam mat.

questions.stem_md:
The figure shows a boy standing on the ground and pushing a wall. Five forces are shown by arrows lettered A to E.

(a) Which two forces form an action-reaction pair? [2]

(b) State the body on which each force of this pair acts. [2]

(c) Name the forces C, D and E. [3]

(d) The boy stays at rest. Which two of the forces balance each other horizontally on him? [2]

(e) Why do the forces of the pair in (a) not cancel? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The forces **A and B**.

**(b)** **A** (push of the boy) acts on the **wall**; **B** (push of the wall) acts on the **boy**.

**(c)** **C** is the **weight** of the boy; **D** is the **normal reaction** of the ground; **E** is the **friction** of the ground on his feet.

**(d)** **B and E** balance each other horizontally on the boy, so he does not slide.

**(e)** They act on **different bodies**, so they cannot cancel.

questions.solution_md: A and B; wall and boy; weight, normal reaction, friction; B and E; different bodies.
